blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: Terminal value: where most DCFs go wrong
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Valuation reps, lesson 5: Terminal value: where most DCFs go wrong.

Here is the number that should bother you every time you build a discounted cash flow, DCF. In a typical five-year model, terminal value often makes up seventy to eighty percent of the total valuation. You spend four weeks modeling revenue growth, margins, and working capital for years one through five, and then one formula, covering everything from year six to infinity, carries most of the weight.

The two methods are the Gordon growth model and the exit multiple. Gordon growth takes your final year free cash flow, grows it by a perpetual rate, usually two to three percent, matching long run gross domestic product, GDP, and divides by the discount rate minus that growth rate. Say your year five free cash flow is 100 million dollars, your discount rate, your weighted average cost of capital, WACC, is nine percent, and perpetual growth is two and a half percent. Terminal value equals 100 million times 1.025, divided by, 0.09 minus 0.025. That is 102.5 million divided by 0.065, which equals roughly 1.58 billion dollars. Discount that back five years at nine percent and you still get around 1.03 billion dollars, dwarfing the four years of explicit cash flow before it.

The one mistake: people pick a growth rate close to the discount rate. Move that perpetual growth from two and a half to three and a half percent, and terminal value jumps to 1.82 billion, a seventeen percent swing from one input nobody stress tested. The formula is mathematically sensitive near that gap, and that sensitivity is exactly where optimism hides.

What this reveals: your valuation is really a bet on one number, the spread between WACC and perpetual growth. What it cannot tell you: whether that spread is even knowable ten years out. This is why you look at analysis first, then technicals, then company against sector, because the DCF output means nothing without that context.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pull up a DCF you've built or seen on Thomson ONE, find the terminal value line, and recalculate it using growth rates of two percent and three percent instead of the base case, noting the swing in final valuation.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Bond Stress, BoC Watch, Oil Slips Lower
blocks.script: Start with rates, because that is what is moving underneath everything else today. The U.S. ten year Treasury yield is sitting near five point three per cent, close to a multidecade high. Bloomberg reports hedge fund founder Ray Dalio is warning Treasuries are vulnerable as China and Japan, two of America's largest foreign creditors, pull back from buying U.S. debt. Dalio says Washington faces a potential debt crisis within three years. That matters here because American yields set the tone for Canadian yields too. On equities, it is a split story. In the U.S., the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq both closed at record highs, tech led again, and Nvidia is closing in on a six trillion dollar market value, up close to thirty per cent this year per Bloomberg. The TSX only inched higher by comparison. Oil is part of the drag: Brent crude fell nearly two per cent to just under ninety nine dollars a barrel, and West Texas Intermediate dropped over two per cent to under eighty eight dollars. The Globe reports resilient Middle East exports and a G7 emergency stockpile release eased supply worries, even with fresh attacks reported near the Strait of Hormuz. The loonie slipped too, trading near seventy cents U.S., down about three and a half per cent over the past month, per the Globe's Before the Bell. Worth flagging for clients asking about cross border shopping or snowbird budgets. On the Bank of Canada, it is on the watch list for good reason. The policy rate has held at two point two five per cent since September, and the next decision lands October twenty eighth alongside a full Monetary Policy Report. Markets are leaning toward another hold, but inflation running above the two per cent target, plus ongoing trade friction with Washington, has some economists talking hike risk instead of cut risk. Tell clients the hold era may not last forever. Statistics Canada releases merchandise trade data for August and the Ivey purchasing managers index today, useful for reading how tariffs are hitting trade flows.
talkingPoints: Bond yields near multidecade highs, fixed income deserves attention, not avoidance.
Oil fell on Middle East export resilience, not demand destruction, different story for energy holdings.
Bank of Canada holds at 2.25 percent, October 28th decision could surprise toward a hike.
Loonie near 70 cents U.S., relevant for snowbird and cross border spending plans.
Toronto home sales down again, watch for ripple effects beyond the GTA.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Mega-mergers, power deals and steel jobs collide
blocks.script: Good evening. Tonight we track the ten companies drawing the most attention across business and markets, with a Canadian lens on energy, autos and steel. Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery. Paramount is the US media company now controlled through Skydance; Warner Bros is the studio behind HBO and CNN. Paramount has closed its roughly 110 billion dollar takeover, creating a new Hollywood giant. Tailwind: scale across film, streaming and news. Headwind: regulators and consumers worry about concentration and higher prices. An evidence-based advisor would say don't chase media consolidation, synergy promises rarely translate cleanly into returns. Google and Constellation Energy. Google is Alphabet's cloud and search arm; Constellation is a major US power and nuclear generator. The two struck a 3.6 gigawatt power deal, with Constellation committing over 4.3 billion dollars in new fleet investment. Tailwind: AI-driven power demand. Headwind: execution and regulatory timelines. Advisors say power-for-AI deals are a durable theme, but valuations already price in plenty of optimism. ATCO and Canadian Utilities, with Nova Scotia's Emera. ATCO is proposing a roughly 35 billion dollar merger of Canadian Utilities with Emera, part of what's being called a 72 billion dollar utility bet. ATCO's Nancy Southern calls it a win-win, creating the pure-play utility analysts favour. Tailwind: scale and simpler structure. Headwind: integration and cross-border approvals. An advisor would call this classic defensive consolidation, fine for income, not growth. CPPIB, AT&T and BlackRock's GIP. Canada's pension giant is joining AT&T and BlackRock's infrastructure arm in a fibre-optic venture funding broadband across 16 US states. Tailwind: steady infrastructure cash flows. Headwind: capital intensity and slow payback. Advisors see textbook pension infrastructure investing, hard for retail investors to replicate. Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs. Stelco is the Hamilton steelmaker owned by US-based Cleveland-Cliffs. Ottawa has given the owner five business days to produce a jobs plan or face possible legal action, while Stelco's exit from galvanized steel has left buyer Cascadia Metals, fresh off a 30 million dollar plant expansion for domestic steel, scrambling. Tailwind: federal pressure could protect jobs. Headwind: trade uncertainty keeps squeezing Canadian steel. Advisors call this a politically exposed, volatile sector. GM in Oshawa and Stellantis in Brampton. GM will end light-duty Silverado production in Oshawa while boosting heavy-duty output, saying jobs should hold. Stellantis workers will vote on strike action after Unifor walked from talks once the automaker confirmed selling its Brampton plant to a defence contractor. Tailwind: heavy-duty demand. Headwind: labour unrest. Advisors treat auto names as cyclical and sensitive to labour headlines. Bombardier.
talkingPoints: Mega-mergers in media and utilities are concentrating power in fewer hands, from Skydance-Warner to ATCO-Emera.
AI-driven power demand, seen in Google's Constellation deal, is reshaping utility investment.
Canadian steel and auto jobs remain politically fraught, with Ottawa pressing Stelco's owner and Stellantis workers readying a strike vote.
Evidence-based advisors keep repeating the same caution: don't trade on merger or breach headlines, focus on fundamentals and diversification.

blocks.script: Start with where the book is moving. Wealth Professional reports that a second generation advisory team in New Brunswick has left its bank-owned dealer for Wellington-Altus, citing teamwork among the deciding factors. Advisor dot ca's morning bulletin shows the same current running at CIBC Wood Gundy and i A Private Wealth, which both picked up new advisor teams this week. If you're weighing independence, the conversation with clients about transition mechanics is getting easier because more peers have already made the move. On the regulatory side, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, or CIRO, posted two dealer amalgamation bulletins yesterday. I P C Investment Corporation is merging with Quadrus Investment Services, and StoneX Financial Canada is combining with R J O'Brien and Associates Canada. If you have clients or referral partners registered under either banner, expect account transfer paperwork in the coming months. Scotia Wealth Management opened a new ultra high net worth service spanning public and private assets, ownership structures, and geography, per Wealth Professional. That's also on my watch list for the program today. For incorporated business owners sitting on significant holding company assets, this is the kind of integrated offering worth benchmarking your own referral network against. On product, Vanguard's Alex Lee makes the case for staying in fixed income despite the volatility, though he flags that active strategies may have an edge right now, Wealth Professional reports. Pair that with a hard number: the RRSP dollar limit for the 2027 tax year is $35,390, up from $33,810 in 2026. The TFSA figure for 2027 is not official until the indexation announcement in November 2026, though the math points toward $7,500. For incorporated professionals juggling salary versus dividends, that RRSP jump matters now, before year end planning. Markets were quiet: the TSX added 16 points while the Nasdaq set another record close, Wealth Professional says. Cenovus is buying an Alberta oilsands rival in a $5.7 billion cash and stock deal adding 45,000 barrels a day of thermal output, closing in December, which lines up with Premier Smith and Prime Minister Carney both saying this next oilsands boom will be managed better than the last. For snowbird clients, Florida's Amendment 3 property tax break skips Canadian owners entirely, Wealth Professional reports, adding another line item to the cross-border ownership conversation ahead of winter departures. Quickly: falling fertility rates could mean slower growth and later retirements for today's accumulators, the Globe reports.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Baby Costs, Hospital Beds, and Language Politics in Manitoba
blocks.script: The biggest Manitoba story today is the squeeze on young families. CBC Manitoba reports prices for baby formula and diapers are climbing in Winnipeg just as donations to assistance programs are dropping, pushing some parents into what advocates call heartbreaking situations, with at least one local program now having to cover more of those costs itself. If you sit on a board for a family or children's charity, that funding gap is worth raising this quarter. On health care, the province says it's adding more than 100 community-based care spaces in Winnipeg for patients who are medically cleared but have nowhere to go, the goal being to free up hospital beds and cut emergency room wait times. It's part of a broader expansion of post-hospital support for homeless and mental health patients. At the Legislature, Premier Wab Kinew has been answering English questions in French for two straight days in question period. A political scientist interviewed by CBC called it an unhealthy politicizing of language, adding friction to a sitting that's already unsettled after a Tory caucus departure last week. On addictions policy, the minister responsible for housing and homelessness says Winnipeg's supervised consumption site is making its surrounding neighbourhood even safer than before, though CBC notes not every nearby resident agrees. On regulation, new provincial legislation would let cannabis retailers remove the window coverings they're currently required to keep up, a safety response after assaults on store staff. Separately, a Manitoba pharmacy owner who reported her own business partner for misusing narcotics has herself been fined fifteen thousand dollars for inadequate oversight of controlled substances, a case worth flagging if you advise anyone in pharmacy or health-sector ownership. On crime, Winnipeg police seized 26 kilograms of cocaine and about $750,000 in cash in a south Winnipeg raid. The RCMP laid 21 new charges in the Bunibonibee drug-trafficking investigation up north. In Osborne Village, a man and woman face charges after assaults that sent two people to hospital. And a U.S. appeals court upheld the conviction in the human smuggling case tied to the 2022 deaths of an Indian family at the Manitoba border near Emerson. Briefly: Uber has permanently banned a driver after an alleged sexual assault in Winnipeg's Weston neighbourhood. Brandon University researchers are sampling frogs and salamanders across the province, expecting to confirm the chytrid fungus, a pathogen with reported presence everywhere around Manitoba, already blamed for the extinction of at least 90 amphibian species worldwide.
talkingPoints: Baby formula and diaper costs are rising in Winnipeg while charity donations fall, a real pressure point for family budgets this fall.
The province's 100-plus new community care beds could ease hospital gridlock, worth watching if you're invested in health infrastructure.
The premier answering in French only has become a genuine flashpoint at the Legislature, not just a language story.
A pharmacy owner who did the right thing by reporting misuse still got fined fifteen thousand dollars, a cautionary tale on regulatory exposure.
The Jets opened the week with a road win over Pittsburgh, 3-2.

blocks.label: Canadian Politics
blocks.title: PQ's Fragile Win, Budget Squeeze, Manitoba Watches
blocks.script: The Parti Québécois has won government, but barely, and that shapes the national unity conversation right as Alberta's referendum vote approaches. The Globe reports Paul St-Pierre Plamondon's party took 59 seats, five short of a majority, on just 28 per cent of the vote, the lowest mandate on record for a governing party. Christine Fréchette is stepping down as CAQ leader after her party was wiped off the map, a result CBC notes hasn't happened to a governing party in Canada since 1987 in New Brunswick. St-Pierre Plamondon says a referendum waits until Trump leaves office in 2029, but CBC reports immigration and Bill 21 could create friction with Ottawa much sooner. Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke with the premier-designate the morning after, stressing cooperation on trade. On the fiscal side, the Globe reports economists say Ottawa's tax revenue bump from higher oil prices has largely already been spent, leaving little room in the fall budget given gasoline tax breaks and the new productivity mega deduction. Defence spending is in focus too. The Parliamentary Budget Officer says direct military spending could reach 163.6 billion dollars by 2035 if Canada hits NATO's 5 per cent of GDP target, CBC reports. Ottawa is also turning its Defence Investment Agency into a Crown corporation, giving it more authority to move faster, though CBC notes critics worry that structure could blur accountability. On immigration, CBC reports Minister Lena Diab appeared unfamiliar, in a Radio-Canada interview, with the Supreme Court ruling anchoring Charter protections for refugees. The Liberals are set to announce next steps on medically assisted dying this week, with Justice Minister Sean Fraser saying government will vote against a private member's bill restricting access for people whose sole condition is a mental disorder. Messaging app Signal says changes to the lawful access bill still won't keep it in Canada, with Firefox's maker echoing the privacy concern. Back home, Manitoba's legislature resumed its fall sitting with the Progressive Conservative opposition scrambling after leader Obby Khan abruptly quit, leaving the party at 19 seats to the NDP's 34.
talkingPoints: PQ's minority government has a historically low mandate, so expect instability, not certainty, on any referendum timeline.

blocks.label: AI & Technology
blocks.title: AI Money Moves: Lambda, Mistral, and Agent Friction
blocks.script:
The biggest AI money story today is Lambda. The Nvidia-backed AI cloud provider is raising up to four billion dollars at a fourteen-point-five billion dollar valuation, ahead of a planned 2027 initial public offering, led by Coatue and Blackstone. Its order backlog jumped from fifteen billion in June to fifty billion in September, largely on a thirty-five billion dollar commitment from Anthropic alone. That's real concentration risk if you've got clients with neocloud exposure.

Anthropic, meanwhile, is giving startups a free year of Claude Team plus a thousand dollars in credits, betting adoption spreads through the companies building on its models, not the model alone.

Mistral released Large 4, a trillion-parameter model the French lab says beats both American and Chinese rivals, though it still needs a cybersecurity and government review before wide release, per the Globe and Mail.

On agents, TechCrunch reports Amazon is now blocking Meta's Muse shopping agent, and Walmart's hit similar snags. Meta, Walmart, Stripe and others are building a shared standard so agents can shop for you without tripping anti-bot defenses, a real friction point before agentic commerce actually scales.

And LibreOffice is now marketing "no AI" as a feature, citing privacy, a sign not everyone wants this baked into their software.
talkingPoints: Lambda's four billion dollar raise leans on one client, Anthropic, that's a concentration risk worth naming.
Anthropic is subsidizing startup adoption with free Claude Team access and credits.
Mistral's trillion-parameter model is Europe's bid to not fall behind the US and China.
Amazon and Walmart are blocking AI shopping agents, agentic commerce has real friction left.

blocks.title: Cartilage Regrowth, Recovery Windows, and New GLP-1 Rules
blocks.script: Start with the one that matters most if you lift or run on older joints. Stanford researchers, publishing in the journal Science, found a protein called 15-PGDH roughly doubles in cartilage as mice age. Block it, and old mice regrew functional knee cartilage, and were far less likely to develop arthritis after ACL-type injuries. Human cartilage from knee replacement patients showed the same early regeneration signals after a week of exposure. This is mouse and tissue-culture work, not a human trial, and some of the inventors hold equity in the company licensing the patent, so treat it as promising, not proven.

blocks.label: Lessons
blocks.title: Holding companies: when they help and when they add cost / Difficult conversations: separating the person from the problem
blocks.script:
Financial Planning Facts, lesson 18: Holding companies: when they help and when they add cost.

A holding company, or Holdco, is just a corporation that owns shares in your operating company, Opco, instead of holding your business assets directly. The dividend from Opco to Holdco moves tax-free under section 112 of the Income Tax Act, because it's an inter-corporate dividend between connected corporations. That's the whole trick. You're not avoiding tax, you're deferring and protecting.

Here's where it helps. Say your Opco in Manitoba has $300,000 of retained earnings sitting as cash, earning interest inside the company. Manitoba's small business rate is 0% federally reduced, so combined with the federal small business rate your Opco pays roughly 9% on the first $500,000 of active income in 2026. But if that $300,000 cash sits in Opco, it's exposed to business creditors, and it pushes up passive investment income, which for 2026 still grinds your $500,000 small business limit dollar for dollar once passive income passes $50,000, fully gone at $150,000. Move that $300,000 to Holdco as a tax-free dividend, and Opco's balance sheet is cleaner for lenders, creditors can't reach it, and you've separated the investment pool from the operating risk.

Where it costs you: a second corporation means a second set of financial statements, a second tax return, separate minute books, and typically another $2,500 to $5,000 a year in accounting and legal fees in Manitoba. If your retained earnings are under roughly $150,000, that cost often outweighs the benefit.

The mistake I see constantly: business owners strip cash into a Holdco after they're already being sued or after a creditor claim exists. That's a fraudulent conveyance, courts will unwind it, and CRA plus creditors both go looking. The protection only works if you move the cash before the liability exists, as routine planning, not as a reaction.

Communication, lesson 18: Difficult conversations: separating the person from the problem.

Picture this. You're on a nonprofit board, and the treasurer wants to cut the youth program budget from 40,000 dollars to 28,000 dollars to cover a shortfall. You think he's being reckless. He thinks you're being sentimental. Within ten minutes, it's not about the number anymore. It's about who's right and who's careless with other people's money.

Roger Fisher and William Ury at the Harvard Negotiation Project named this problem in Getting to Yes, back in 1981: people fuse the issue with the identity of the person raising it. Their fix is one sentence: separate the people from the problem. You treat the person as someone you're working alongside, and you put the problem on the table in front of both of you, not between you.

Here's how that plays out with the 12,000 dollar gap. Instead of saying "you're gutting the program," you say, "we have a 12,000 dollar gap, and I want to find it without cutting the mentoring hours. What are you protecting when you propose this cut, and what am I protecting when I resist it?" Now you're both looking at the same number, with two different interests on the table: his interest is solvency, yours is program continuity. That's a problem you can solve together. Maybe you find 8,000 dollars in deferred vendor payments and split the remaining 4,000 across two fiscal quarters.

The mistake almost everyone makes, documented by Douglas Stone, Bruce Patton, and Sheila Heen in Difficult Conversations, is skipping straight to the content fight while ignoring the identity fight underneath it: am I competent, am I a good person, am I in control. If you don't name that layer, it leaks into every sentence about the budget.

Today's task: think of one live disagreement you're avoiding. Write the issue in one line, then write each person's underlying interest in one line each. Do it before you talk to anyone.
talkingPoints: Financial Planning Facts: Pull one client's Opco balance sheet, total the retained earnings sitting as cash or investments, and flag whether it's past $150,000, the point where a Holdco conversation is worth having this month.
Communication: Pick one current disagreement and write three lines: the issue in neutral language, your interest, and the other person's likely interest, before your next conversation with them.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Bond Contagion Fears Rattle Europe, Loonie Slides
blocks.script:
Start with what is rattling global bond markets right now, because it will come up with clients today. French, Italian, Belgian and Greek government bonds, which normally move together, broke apart on Thursday and sold off hard at the same time. Bloomberg reports a Morgan Stanley portfolio manager says traders are seeing the first signs of contagion, the word everyone remembers from Europe's debt crisis fifteen years ago. The euro fell to its weakest level in seventeen months against the US dollar on the back of it. That dollar strength spilled into Canada too. The Globe and Mail reports the loonie touched an eighteen month low, with speculators raising bearish bets, even as it traded close to 70 US cents.

None of that stopped Canadian and US equities. The TSX closed up nearly one percent, just above 35,500. The S&P 500 added about three quarters of a percent, the Nasdaq better than one percent. That follows Friday's softer US jobs data, which pared back bets on another Federal Reserve hike this month, with traders now pricing less than a one in four chance.

On the Bank of Canada, the overnight rate has been held at 2.25 percent since September 2, the seventh straight hold. The next announcement is October 28, with a full Monetary Policy Report attached. That one matters, because inflation is stuck near three percent and oil prices are elevated, so markets are genuinely split between another hold and a surprise hike.

On jobs, Statistics Canada's most recent report showed the economy lost 42,000 positions in August, ending a hot four month run of hiring, while the unemployment rate held at 6.4 percent.

In energy, oil slipped again toward 90 dollars US, as the G7 taps emergency reserves to calm supply nerves. Calgary's Suncor is selling its stakes in three Newfoundland offshore fields to Ithaca Energy for 1.2 billion dollars. Gold is holding just above 4,160 dollars an ounce, still near record highs.
talkingPoints: Watch the Bank of Canada's October 28 decision, a hike is back on the table, not just a hold.
Euro zone bond stress is a real risk to watch, it already pushed our dollar to an eighteen month low.
TSX and Wall Street keep grinding higher even with the bond noise, don't let clients overreact.
August's jobs loss shows the labour market cooling, worth flagging for anyone nervous about their own position.
Oil near 90 dollars and G7 reserve releases are capping energy price spikes for now.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Utility Mega-Deal Leads Busy Week For Dealmakers
blocks.script: Good evening. Tonight we're tracking the companies drawing the most attention over the past two days, led by a wave of mergers and takeover activity across Canada's utility, energy and cannabis sectors. Emera and Canadian Utilities: Emera is the Halifax-based utility behind Nova Scotia Power, with operations across North America and the Caribbean. It has made a friendly all-stock bid for Canadian Utilities, the Alberta company at the heart of the ATCO group, in a deal the Globe and Mail values near 35 billion dollars. The tailwind is scale, since the merger would create one of the 20 largest utilities in North America. The headwind is the complexity of winning regulatory approval across multiple jurisdictions. An evidence-based advisor would tell clients utility mergers this size take months to clear, so patience matters more than chasing the stock now. Cenovus and Athabasca Oil: Cenovus is one of Canada's largest integrated oil producers, and it has agreed to buy oilsands player Athabasca Oil as part of a growth push. The Globe notes the deal has analysts scouting a new generation of oil patch takeover targets. The tailwind is consolidation appetite in the oilsands; the headwind is ongoing commodity price volatility. An advisor would caution against chasing takeover rumours in small-cap energy names, since that is speculation, not investing. Curaleaf and Aurora Cannabis: Curaleaf is a major US cannabis operator that has sweetened its offer for Toronto-based Aurora Cannabis, now targeting roughly five US dollars a share. The tailwind is sector consolidation finally offering shareholders an exit; the headwind is Aurora's long record of value destruction since legalization. An advisor would frame this as a one-time event to evaluate, not a long-term cannabis thesis. Cohere: The Toronto AI company unveiled a new version of its North platform with more agentic features, aimed at winning corporate and government customers. The tailwind is strong enterprise AI demand; the headwind is intense competition from much larger global rivals. An advisor would note Cohere is still private, so there is no direct public market way in yet. Nutrien: The Saskatchewan fertilizer giant is indefinitely shutting its Trinidad nitrogen operations due to natural gas supply constraints. That's a near-term headwind for volumes, though global fertilizer demand remains a longer-term tailwind. An advisor would call this a contained operational issue rather than a reason to rethink the stock.
talkingPoints: Watch for regulatory developments on the Emera-Canadian Utilities merger and further oil patch deals following Cenovus-Athabasca.
Aurora Cannabis shareholders now face a decision on Curaleaf's richer offer.

blocks.title: Election Discontent, Tesla's Court Fight, Hydro's Big Loss
blocks.script: Start with the municipal election, because it's the conversation every client is having right now. A new Abacus Data poll, commissioned by the Free Press, finds half of Winnipeggers think the city is heading in the wrong direction, with only twenty one percent saying it's on the right track. Four in ten say they get poor value for their property tax dollars. That discontent is shaping the mayoral race: challenger Kevin Klein is pledging to restore the city ombudsman position, cut more than two decades ago, while incumbent Scott Gillingham has leaned softer, proposing a park along the Seine River. Out in Waverley West, the city's biggest and fastest growing ward, five candidates are running on how to manage that growth, and province wide, the Association of Manitoba Municipalities says acclamations are down this year, meaning more communities actually have a choice on the ballot. Advance voting opened Monday. On the Tesla file, now in court. Tesla's lawyers argued in front of a Manitoba Court of King's Bench judge that the province's decision to cut the company from the EV rebate program was politically motivated and unfair, pointing to Premier Wab Kinew's own past comments tying the exclusion to Elon Musk's politics. The province counters that it was a budget decision and not reviewable by the courts. That rebate was worth up to four thousand dollars a vehicle. Manitoba Hydro is on the watch list, and it had a rough year. The Crown corporation's annual report shows a four hundred forty six million dollar loss for twenty twenty five, twenty six, driven by drought that forced Hydro to import almost as much power as it exported. The energy regulator is still weighing a plan to free up over a quarter of Hydro's generating capacity, including a three billion dollar gas plant expansion in Brandon. Two government bills landed this week. One lets cannabis stores remove window coverings, after reports of assaults on staff. The other strengthens protections for survivors of intimate partner violence. In Morden, the family of a young woman who died after a dental procedure is suing the dentist and clinic over a local anesthetic injected into a blood vessel. On crime and courts: Manitoba's Court of Appeal ruled the People's Party of Canada partly liable in a Winnipeg defamation case. RCMP seized thirteen guns and twenty thousand rounds of ammunition from two homes in West St. Paul.

Good evening. We start in Ottawa, where sources tell the Globe and Mail the federal government plans to turn its year-old Defence Investment Agency into a Crown corporation. CBC reports the move is meant to break a long-standing logjam in Canada's defence procurement system. The change would hand chief executive Doug Guzman far more authority over purchasing decisions, though it raises questions about oversight and accountability that officials have yet to fully answer.

Security concerns are also in focus after Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree said Canadian law enforcement may get involved in the case of an alleged NATO spy once a Belgian inquiry concludes. Anandasangaree told CBC the case points to gaps in Canada's security screening that need addressing, with Canadian departments now facing scrutiny over the person's activities here.

The Department of National Defence confirmed two members of the Canadian Armed Forces were arrested by Toronto police as part of a probe into organized crime, kidnapping and firearms theft. DND says it is cooperating with the investigation.

In Alberta, MPs are reacting to a Globe and Mail investigation showing separatist leaders met with Republican political operatives and offered access to provincial resources, including fresh water, forestry and mining, in exchange for American support. Calgary Liberal MP Corey Hogan said Canada may need to review laws around this kind of freelance diplomacy, though he stopped short of calling it treasonous.

And on the world stage, mapmakers are grappling with a presidential edict from Donald Trump over naming conventions on Lake Ontario, with a United Nations group meeting this month to look at bringing order to how such disputes are handled globally.

blocks.label: Health & Fitness
blocks.title: Fasting Study Shows Day-Three Turning Point
blocks.script: The biggest health story today is about fasting, and it matters if you train. Scientists at Queen Mary University of London monitored 12 healthy volunteers during a seven day water-only fast, tracking roughly 3,000 proteins circulating in the bloodstream. The body quickly shifted from burning glucose to burning fat within the first two to three days of fasting, but the most notable biological changes only appeared after about three days without calories. The findings are published in Nature Metabolism, but with only twelve people, call it early stage, not a prescription. One flag if you lift: participants lost an average of 5.7 kilograms, including both fat and lean tissue, and while most of the lean tissue loss returned once eating resumed, you are down real muscle during the fast itself.

blocks.script: The biggest development story this week: new research reported by ScienceDaily found that stimulating the vagus nerve right after a mouse practices a new motor skill helped that skill stick for good, more than practice alone. The effect tracked with rhythmic changes in brain blood vessels, suggesting the body sends signals that help the brain lock in new learning. It is mice, not toddlers, but it strengthens the case that timing and rest after practice matter for how skills become permanent. blocks.title: Employment data: participation, unemployment, wage growth, and what moves the Bank / GRIP and eligible dividend capacity / The confident no: declining a request and keeping the relationship
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Macro & rates, lesson 4: Employment data: participation, unemployment, wage growth, and what moves the Bank.

The unemployment rate can move in the right direction for the wrong reason, and that's the detail almost everyone skips before calling a jobs report good news.

Three numbers matter here, not one. The unemployment rate: people without work, actively looking, as a share of the labour force. The participation rate: the share of the working age population either employed or looking. And wage growth: average hourly earnings, year over year.

Take Statistics Canada's Labour Force Survey for September 2026. Unemployment ticked up to 6.6 percent from 6.5. On its own that reads as softening. But participation also fell, to 65.0 percent from 65.3. That means part of the rise in unemployment wasn't people losing jobs, it was fewer people in the labour force to begin with, so some who'd normally be counted as unemployed simply stopped looking and dropped out of the denominator. Read unemployment without participation and you misjudge how much real slack opened up.

Wage growth that same month ran 3.7 percent year over year. That's the number the Bank of Canada leans on hardest, because wages feed directly into services inflation, the sticky component core measures struggle to shake. The Bank's reaction function: unemployment and participation tell it about slack, wage growth tells it whether that slack is translating into price pressure through labour costs.

The one mistake: treating a single month's print as a trend. These numbers get revised, and one release can be noise from a strike, a weather event, or a survey quirk. The Bank watches a three month moving average of wage growth specifically to filter that out.

On Thomson ONE, the Labour Force Survey sits in the economic release calendar under Canada, and the Bank's wage common measure is a separate series worth cross referencing against the headline average hourly earnings number.

What this data reveals: real time pressure on the labour market the Bank has to weigh against its inflation mandate. What it cannot do: tell you which sectors are driving it, or whether one month's surprise survives revision. Use it as a direction check, not a verdict.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 17: GRIP and eligible dividend capacity.

If a Manitoba corporation pays an eligible dividend with no General Rate Income Pool to back it, the corporation faces Part III.1 tax right now, in 2026, at 20 percent of the excess. That's the whole lesson in one sentence: eligible dividends require eligible dividend capacity, and that capacity has a name, GRIP, General Rate Income Pool.

Here's what builds it. Income taxed at the small business deduction rate doesn't count. In Manitoba for 2026, the combined federal and provincial small business rate is 9 percent, federal 9, Manitoba 0, on the first 500,000 dollars of active income. That income never touches GRIP. Income taxed at the general corporate rate does count. Manitoba's general rate is 12 percent, federal is 15, combined 27 percent for 2026. GRIP grows by 72 percent of that general-rate income, a factor that's been fixed since 2019.

Worked example. Your incorporated physician client earns 600,000 dollars of active business income. 500,000 is taxed at the 9 percent small business rate, that chunk adds nothing to GRIP. The remaining 100,000 is taxed at the 27 percent general rate. GRIP addition equals 72 percent of 100,000, which is 72,000 dollars. That 72,000 is now available to flow out as an eligible dividend, taxed in the shareholder's hands at the lower eligible rate with the enhanced dividend tax credit, instead of the ineligible rate.

The mistake. Advisors and bookkeepers assume retained earnings equals dividend capacity. It doesn't. A corporation can show 400,000 in retained earnings and have zero GRIP if all of it came from small business deduction income. Declare an eligible dividend against a zero GRIP balance and CRA reclassifies the excess, applying that 20 percent Part III.1 tax on top of the personal tax your client already paid.

Today's task. Pull Schedule 53 from the corporation's last filed T2 and confirm the current GRIP balance before you recommend any dividend mix this quarter.

Communication, lesson 17: The confident no: declining a request and keeping the relationship.

William Ury spent decades inside the Camp David talks and corporate boardrooms, and he says the costliest word in negotiation isn't "no," it's the mushy maybe that follows a bad no. In his book "The Power of a Positive No," he lays out a three part structure: yes, no, yes. You open with the yes behind your no, the thing you actually support. Then you deliver the no itself, short, not apologetic. Then you close with a yes, an alternative that keeps the door open.

Here's the real numbers. A client emails you on a Tuesday. He wants his LinkedIn video series turned around in three days instead of the ten you agreed, same 2,100 dollar fee, because he's speaking at a conference Friday. You say: "Yes, I want you walking into that room with strong video, that matters." That's yes one. Then: "I can't deliver broadcast quality in three days without cutting the editing pass, so no to that timeline at this price." That's the no. Then: "I can get you a rough cut in five days for a rush fee of 900 dollars, bringing it to 3,000 total." That's yes two. He now has a real choice instead of a guilt trip.

The mistake almost everyone makes is stacking justifications. Vanessa Bohns, a Cornell researcher who studies compliance, found that people routinely overestimate how upset someone gets when refused, so they overcompensate with three or four reasons. Each extra reason reads as a weak point the other person can push against. One reason, stated once, holds. Four reasons invite negotiation over which one is weakest.

Today's practice: write out one real request you need to decline this week, in the yes, no, yes structure, under sixty words total, and send it before the day ends.

Worked example. Your incorporated physician client earns 600,000 dollars of active business income. 500,000 is taxed at the 9 percent small business rate, that chunk adds nothing to GRIP. The remaining 100,000 is taxed at the 27 percent general rate. GRIP addition equals 72 percent of 100,000, which is 72,000 dollars. That 72,000 is now available to flow out as an eligible dividend, taxed in the shareholder's hands at the lower eligible rate with the enhanced dividend tax credit, instead of the ineligible rate.

The mistake. Advisors and bookkeepers assume retained earnings equals dividend capacity. It doesn't. A corporation can show 400,000 in retained earnings and have zero GRIP if all of it came from small business deduction income. Declare an eligible dividend against a zero GRIP balance and CRA reclassifies the excess, applying that 20 percent Part III.1 tax on top of the personal tax your client already paid.

Today's task. Pull Schedule 53 from the corporation's last filed T2 and confirm the current GRIP balance before you recommend any dividend mix this quarter.

lessons.label: Communication
lessons.title: The confident no: declining a request and keeping the relationship
lessons.script:
William Ury spent decades inside the Camp David talks and corporate boardrooms, and he says the costliest word in negotiation isn't "no," it's the mushy maybe that follows a bad no. In his book "The Power of a Positive No," he lays out a three part structure: yes, no, yes. You open with the yes behind your no, the thing you actually support. Then you deliver the no itself, short, not apologetic. Then you close with a yes, an alternative that keeps the door open.

Here's the real numbers. A client emails you on a Tuesday. He wants his LinkedIn video series turned around in three days instead of the ten you agreed, same 2,100 dollar fee, because he's speaking at a conference Friday. You say: "Yes, I want you walking into that room with strong video, that matters." That's yes one. Then: "I can't deliver broadcast quality in three days without cutting the editing pass, so no to that timeline at this price." That's the no. Then: "I can get you a rough cut in five days for a rush fee of 900 dollars, bringing it to 3,000 total." That's yes two. He now has a real choice instead of a guilt trip.

The mistake almost everyone makes is stacking justifications. Vanessa Bohns, a Cornell researcher who studies compliance, found that people routinely overestimate how upset someone gets when refused, so they overcompensate with three or four reasons. Each extra reason reads as a weak point the other person can push against. One reason, stated once, holds. Four reasons invite negotiation over which one is weakest.

Today's practice: write out one real request you need to decline this week, in the yes, no, yes structure, under sixty words total, and send it before the day ends.
lessons.task: Pick one pending request you've been avoiding, write the yes, no, yes version in under sixty words, and send it today.
lessons.drill: Record yourself delivering a decline out loud in under thirty seconds, then play it back against three checks: did you state a clear yes before the no, did the no land in one sentence without stacked reasons, did you offer one concrete alternative with a number or date attached. Score one point per check. Three out of three is a pass; anything stacking more than one reason before the no is an automatic fail regardless of the other scores.

blocks.label: Markets & Economy
blocks.title: Oil Falls, Stocks Climb, Bank of Canada Stays Split
blocks.script:
Start with oil, because it sets the tone for everything else today. The Globe and Mail reports crude is steadying after a run of selling, with Middle Eastern crude exports rising and the Group of Seven, the G7, moving to release strategic stocks. Saudi Aramco has unexpectedly cut its official selling prices, which is usually a signal the kingdom expects demand to soften, not strengthen. This morning's snapshot has oil down one point nine percent to ninety one dollars and eleven cents, extending a stretch of lower prices. For clients worried about another inflation spike from energy, this is the opposite story: more supply hitting the market, not less.

That ties into the broader premarket picture. The Globe reports world shares advanced overnight and oil prices fell as worries over inflation ease, and you can see it in today's numbers. The Toronto Stock Exchange is up zero point nine nine percent to thirty five thousand five hundred two. The S&P 500 is up zero point seven three percent to seven thousand seven hundred twenty two. The Dow is up zero point four nine percent. The Nasdaq leads, up one point one nine percent to twenty seven thousand one hundred ninety. Gold, by contrast, is down nearly one percent to four thousand one hundred sixty two dollars, which tells you some of the safety bid that's been in gold all year is coming off as risk appetite returns.

The Canadian dollar is softer, down zero point two percent to seventy point two cents US. Worth flagging for clients with cross border spending or snowbird plans, the loonie has not been strengthening even as Canadian equities do well.

There's a bigger story under the surface in Europe you should be ready to speak to. Bloomberg's Markets Daily is flagging early signs of contagion in European bond markets, with France, Italy, Belgium and Greece all seeing a selloff that broke the pattern of bonds moving together. The euro fell to its weakest level in seventeen months against the US dollar. A portfolio manager at Brandywine Global told Bloomberg it's probably too early to call a bottom. If a client asks why their global or international holdings looked shaky, European sovereign stress is the answer.

Closer to home, and this is one for any client who thinks they can beat the index by picking names. The Globe's Inside the Market column makes the case that it is a terrible time to be a stock picker, pointing out that at no point this century have the odds of picking winning stocks been worse. That's a calm way to reinforce diversification conversations without sounding like you're dodging the question.

On the other end of the sentiment spectrum, the British brokerage Panmure Liberum put out a forecast worth mentioning, even as an outlier. They're calling for the S&P 500 to fall to five thousand, more than thirty five percent below its last close, and warning the bull run is nearing its end. I wouldn't reposition a portfolio off one house's call, but it's a useful conversation piece if a client brings up the headline, because it shows how wide the range of professional opinion actually is right now.

For anyone looking for actionable ideas, the Globe has a list out today of fourteen dividend and value stocks worth considering, framed as a way to add flexibility and reduce volatility rather than chase momentum names. Worth a look before your next client call. And on the practice side, there's a good piece today on planning a family wealth meeting, with five steps advisors can use. The core point is that a successful first meeting is less about revealing numbers and more about understanding the client's goals and the family's dynamics. If you've got a multi generational relationship on your book, that's worth rereading this week.

Now to the Bank of Canada, which is on the watch list and should be on yours too. The Bank held its policy rate at two point two five percent on September second, the seventh straight hold, with the overnight rate unchanged for nearly a year. The next decision is October twenty eighth, and it comes with a full Monetary Policy Report. Markets are not settled on the outcome. With headline inflation sitting around three percent and core around two percent, and oil and gas prices adding pressure underneath, pricing now shows a real chance of a hike rather than another hold. That's a shift from earlier this year, when cuts were still being debated. If clients ask whether rates are going up or down from here, the honest answer is the Bank itself has left both doors open.

Statistics Canada's jobs report for September lands this Friday, and it matters more than usual because it's the first full month of data since new US tariffs, under what's called Section 338, took effect in August. Economists at RBC expect employment rose by a modest five thousand, with the unemployment rate holding around six point four percent, still elevated but noticeably better than a year ago. On growth, GDP is tracking near two percent annualized in the third quarter, following a stronger three point three percent gain in the second. RBC estimates roughly zero point four percent of GDP, and related employment, sits in sectors directly hit by the tariff list, contained but real.

On housing, mortgage pricing is still elevated even with the Bank on hold. Four year fixed insured rates are sitting around four point seven nine percent, uninsured closer to five point three one percent, per nesto's tracking. That's the backdrop for any client weighing a renewal this fall, the Bank's hold has not translated into meaningfully cheaper fixed rate borrowing.

On the fiscal side, Ottawa's own figures show Canada still outpacing the US on jobs per capita since early last year, and the unemployment rate has come down from last summer's peak. That's the government's framing for its own policy, useful context if a client only cites the negative headlines.
talkingPoints: Oil is lower and supply is rising, that undercuts the inflation scare story for now.
The Bank of Canada's October twenty eighth decision is genuinely live, hold or hike are both on the table.
European bond stress in France and Italy is worth watching if you hold international fixed income.
It is a bad environment for stock picking, lean on that to reinforce diversified portfolios.
Mortgage renewals are not getting cheaper just because the Bank is on hold.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Suncor's East Coast Exit Leads A Busy Week
blocks.script:
Suncor Energy is the story with the most weight behind it right now. This is Calgary's oil sands giant, one of the biggest integrated producers in the country, and the Globe and Mail reports it is selling stakes in three Canadian East Coast projects, Terra Nova, White Rose and West White Rose, to Ithaca Energy PLC for up to one point five billion dollars. The sale marks a major pullback from a region where Suncor has been active for decades. The tailwind is simple: that cash lets Suncor concentrate capital on its core oil sands assets and strengthen the balance sheet. The headwind is what the exit signals, a shrinking Canadian offshore footprint at a moment when Ottawa keeps tightening the regulatory screws on oil sands emissions. An evidence-based advisor tells you not to chase this stock on deal headlines, you likely already own Suncor through any broad Canadian equity index fund, so there is no need to make a fresh single-name bet on the back of one transaction.

OpenAI is next, and it shows up here through the new Trump AI task force story that the Globe and CBC both covered this week. OpenAI is the maker of ChatGPT, the most widely used consumer AI product on the planet, run by Sam Altman. It is now one of the companies Washington is calling a Super Intelligence Company, folded into Jay Clayton's new task force, and separately the Federal Trade Commission under chair Andrew Ferguson has an open investigation into the firm. Sam Altman advocates for federal regulations on advanced AI models. That advocacy is the tailwind, a seat at the table shaping rules before rivals do. The headwind is that open FTC inquiry and a hundred and twenty day policy review hanging over the whole industry. An evidence-based advisor reminds you OpenAI has no public ticker, so any exposure you have is indirect, through the big technology names in your index fund, not through buying the company itself.

Anthropic sits right beside it in the same story. This is the maker of the Claude chatbot, OpenAI's chief rival in frontier AI models, led by Dario Amodei. Amodei also advocates for federal regulations on advanced AI models, and like OpenAI, Anthropic is named in the FTC's active scrutiny alongside the research group METR. The tailwind is reputational, positioning itself as the safety-first lab could matter if Washington's new task force leans toward stricter rules that favour incumbents with compliance muscle. The headwind is the same regulatory uncertainty facing the whole sector, plus intense competitive spending from better-capitalized rivals. An evidence-based advisor says the same thing here as with OpenAI: private company, no shares to buy, resist the urge to find a side door into the name.

BT Group is the UK's largest telecom and broadband provider, and the BBC reports it has agreed a rescue deal to buy broadband operator TalkTalk. The takeover still needs to be approved by the regulator, but would give certainty to TalkTalk's millions of customers. The tailwind for BT is consolidation, fewer competitors, millions of new subscribers, and potential cost savings from combining networks. The headwind is regulatory approval risk and the cost of absorbing a company that needed rescuing in the first place. An evidence-based advisor notes this is a UK domestic story with limited read-through for a Canadian portfolio, so if you hold it at all it is likely a small sliver inside an international developed markets fund, not a reason to act today.

TalkTalk is the other half of that deal, a UK broadband operator that had been under financial strain for years. The BBC's reporting frames this as a rescue, not a bidding war, which tells you which direction the leverage ran in that negotiation. The tailwind is obvious, the deal removes the risk of insolvency and gives customers continuity of service. The headwind is just as obvious, a rescue price rarely rewards existing shareholders the way a competitive auction would. An evidence-based advisor uses this as a teaching moment: distressed turnaround stories look tempting but the math usually favours the acquirer, not the public shareholders hoping for a rebound.

Ithaca Energy PLC is the buyer in that Suncor transaction, a UK-listed oil and gas producer built on North Sea assets that is now expanding into Atlantic Canada. Picking up Terra Nova, White Rose and West White Rose for up to one point five billion dollars is a straight growth-through-acquisition move into a basin it did not previously operate in. The tailwind is diversification into producing Canadian offshore assets at a moment when global buyers still see value there. The headwind is execution risk, operating unfamiliar offshore fields under Canadian regulation is harder than running a spreadsheet. An evidence-based advisor says this deal shows global capital still prices Canadian offshore oil fairly, but one cross-border transaction is not a reason to add a UK oil ticker to your holdings.

Questerre Energy Corp is a Calgary-based junior that has spent years holding Utica shale gas licences inside Quebec's borders. The Globe reports Quebec is having second thoughts on its oil and gas development ban, with the question of whether hydropower-rich Quebec needs its own oil and gas, and two party leaders showing openness to revisit shale gas development through this election campaign. The tailwind for a name like Questerre is political reversal, any softening of the ban reopens a path to monetizing those stranded licences. The headwind is years of lawsuits and public resistance to fracking that has not gone away just because an election is happening. An evidence-based advisor calls this a speculative, binary political bet, size it like one if you touch it at all.

Molagri closes the list, a Toronto biotech startup profiled in the Globe's Rob Magazine. The company wants to help farmers stay ahead of mutating pests and save pollinators, essentially building crop protection that does not kill the bees crops depend on. The tailwind is a genuinely large addressable market, global food security and collapsing pollinator populations are both real problems investors want exposure to. The headwind is that it is early stage and unproven at commercial scale, and agricultural biotech approvals move slowly through regulators. An evidence-based advisor treats this as venture capital territory, interesting to watch, not a position for money you need in the next decade.

No mentions turned up this cycle for the Bank of Canada rate decision, Dimensional Fund Advisors, Scotia Wealth Management, Manitoba Hydro, United Way Winnipeg, the Jets or the Blue Bombers in the business and markets coverage reviewed here, so nothing to flag from that watch list today.

blocks.title: TFSA Jumps, RRSP Confirmed, CCPC Math Matters Now
blocks.script:
Start with the number that touches every planning conversation you'll have this month. The Canada Revenue Agency has confirmed the 2027 Registered Retirement Savings Plan dollar limit at 35,390 dollars, up 1,580 dollars from 33,810 this year, and that increase is tied to average wage growth, not inflation. One analysis built on the CRA's own formula puts the earned income needed to hit that maximum at roughly 196,611 dollars in 2026. The Tax-Free Savings Account number is still pending, but the CRA has confirmed the 2026 limit holds at 7,000 dollars, and the Globe and Mail's read of the indexing formula points to a jump to 7,500 dollars in 2027, the fifth increase since the account launched in 2009. Start that conversation with clients now, don't wait for the November announcement.

That RRSP earned income test is also why the salary versus dividend debate inside a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation, a CCPC, keeps resurfacing. A physician or business owner who pays themselves only in dividends builds no RRSP room at all. With passive income still clawing back the small business deduction once a corporation earns past 50,000 dollars in investment income, this is the week to run the salary top-up numbers before year end.

On regulation, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, CIRO, sanctioned Scotia Securities Incorporated in August, part of the Scotiabank wealth group, and that one's on the watch list given the Scotia Wealth Management name. Across the whole self-regulator, CIRO handed out more than 15 million dollars in sanctions during fiscal 2026, with outside business activity disclosure and referral arrangement gaps named as recurring findings. If you're licensed through the Manitoba Securities Commission, note that Manitoba and British Columbia remain the two provinces still outside the national handover of registration functions to CIRO, so provincial sign-off still applies here in ways it no longer does in Ontario.

Also on the watch list, the Bank of Canada. Advisor.ca and Investment Executive both flag new research this morning showing tariffs are pushing prices up less than feared, because retailers are compressing margins and shoppers are substituting cheaper goods, the backdrop heading into the next rate call.

On the practice side, the Globe and Mail reports about one third of Canadians aged 18 to 44 now carry a second income stream on top of a full time job. That's a filing problem as much as a planning one. Gig income is self-employment income, it can trigger its own GST or HST registration, and it changes Canada Pension Plan contribution math. Ask your younger clients directly if they're freelancing on the side, it affects their contribution room calculations.

Wealth Professional covers a new platform letting people trade on disputed facts that have already happened, flipping the usual prediction market model. Treat it like any new retail speculation product, ask whether the money is savings or investment, and keep it away from registered accounts.

Briefly, the Globe reports StubHub is still missing arbitration fee deadlines after the arbitration body asked to have its name pulled from the user agreement. It's a clean example for compliance conversations about why your own firm's dispute resolution clause gets read closely.

And the Globe's profile of a 33 year old who bought her Vancouver condo in her mid-20s by maximizing savings is worth using with any client buying a first home today. The First Home Savings Account didn't exist when she bought. Stacking it with the Home Buyers' Plan is now the better order of operations.

Quick product note: Harvest, Mackenzie and Manulife all launched new exchange traded funds this week, alongside changes from CI Global Asset Management and ivari, continuing the shift toward narrow, targeted mandates over broad index products.

Dividend-only compensation in a CCPC means zero RRSP room, check the salary mix now.
CIRO just sanctioned a Scotia Securities entity, outside business activity remains the hot exam topic.
Manitoba is still outside the CIRO registration handover, provincial rules still apply here.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Winnipeg mayoral race, trust, and reconciliation fallout
blocks.script:
The Southern Chiefs' Organization came out this morning with a formal condemnation of the Winnipeg Sun, and it is tangled up directly in the mayoral race. On October 4, the Sun published a column entitled "Grave misdirection: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence," suggesting the deaths of Indigenous children at residential schools have been mischaracterized. The column states that each death is a tragedy, but none is evidence of an atrocity, citing as examples the death of one child from bronchitis and another by lightning. The publication four days after the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation led to a formal statement of condemnation from the Southern Chiefs' Organization, which represents 33 Anishinaabe and Dakota First Nations in Manitoba. SCO Grand Chief Jerry Daniels said survivors and their families should not be forced, yet again, to prove what happened to them or defend the children who never came home, and that thousands of children died while attending residential schools. The complication for you is the Sun's publisher partner: that's Kevin Klein, a former city councillor and provincial cabinet minister who is now a candidate for mayor of Winnipeg. Expect this to follow him through the rest of the campaign, and expect clients to ask about it.

That mayoral race already has its own drama this week. Per CBC, mayoral hopeful Mike Vogiatzakis claims rival candidate Kevin Klein's campaign offered an inducement to withdraw from the city's mayoral race, and Klein's camp is making the same accusation back at Vogiatzakis. With a crowded field on the ballot for the October 28th vote, and Winnipeg's last sitting mayor to lose re-election going back to 1956, these inducement allegations are the kind of thing that could shape coverage right through voting day.

Underneath all of that sits a trust problem that is shaping the whole campaign. Crime and safety issues are dominating this municipal election cycle, and a recent survey suggests many people aren't confident police will respond promptly if they need help. Specifically, a survey conducted for CBC News in August found 45 per cent of respondents in Winnipeg agreed they trust police to respond quickly if they need help, with 7 per cent agreeing strongly and 38 per cent agreeing somewhat. About a quarter were unsure, around a quarter disagreed somewhat, and five per cent disagreed strongly. That is the number every mayoral candidate is now running against, and it is worth knowing if the topic comes up at a client meeting this week.

On a quieter note, hundreds marched from The Forks to Portage and Main Sunday in a memorial walk honouring Alaya McIvor, a prominent advocate for missing and murdered Indigenous women, girls, and two spirit people. It is the kind of community moment that often comes up in conversation this week, especially with anyone active in reconciliation or non-profit work.

Separately, police have made an arrest in a long-unsolved violent case. A 27-year-old man is facing several charges more than four years after a 2022 shooting in the lobby of a Winnipeg apartment building that left a man with life-altering injuries. It is a reminder that some of the city's older violent files do eventually move, even years later.

On the legal front, there is a ruling with real implications for anyone with First Nations economic development exposure. A federal judge recently said the way Canada has continued to shirk its responsibilities to a group of Manitoba First Nations since signing a landmark agreement meant to resolve historic treaty land shortages is simply not acceptable. The judge's phrase was blunt: this is not reconciliation. If you or a board colleague has any involvement with First Nations land claims or treaty settlement trusts, this is one to flag, because it signals the federal government still has exposure on a file many assumed was closed.

And a result that will be on a lot of minds at the Monday morning meeting, win or lose. The Blue Bombers, who are on plenty of watch lists in this city, took a beating on the road. Tyson Philpot added three more milestones to an already remarkable season Saturday night, coupled with the Montreal Alouettes clinching the East Division in a dominant 37-10 victory over the Winnipeg Blue Bombers in front of a sellout crowd of 23,035 at Percival Molson Stadium. The coach's own line afterward was simple: they beat us pretty good.

Finally, something lighter for the end of your meetings this week. A gigantic gourd weighing 782 kilograms smashed the record for the province's largest recorded pumpkin at the Roland Pumpkin Fair, in the village of Roland, about 80 kilometres southwest of Winnipeg, on Saturday. That is over seventeen hundred pounds, good trivia for your next client dinner.

blocks.title: Tariffs, Arctic Drills, and a Surveillance Bill Backlash
blocks.script:
The biggest open question for Manitoba exporters right now is what happens on December 31st. The Globe and Mail reports that China suspended a 100 per cent tariff on peas and canola meal, and 25 per cent levies on lobster and crabs as part of the Carney-Xi meeting in January, and these suspensions are currently slated to end after Dec. 31. There is no renewal confirmed. Unresolved barriers remain for pork, which faces a 25 per cent tariff, and canola oil still carries a 100 per cent tariff. A former Global Affairs China hand told the Globe the whole package is tangled up with Ottawa's handling of Chinese steel, which matters because Carney's challenge is offering China more steel access given US demands in the current trade dispute between the United States and Canada. For canola growers in your client base, that's three months of hoping a side deal on steel does not collapse a deal on peas.

On defence, CBC reports Canadian troops ran into real trouble during a major exercise in Alaska this fall, battling frostbite, failing batteries, and communications gaps. They hit their training objectives, but the exercise exposed how far the Forces have to go to deliver the credible Arctic combat capability Ottawa keeps promising in budget documents. That's relevant if you're watching defence procurement stocks or federal capital spending commitments tied to Arctic sovereignty.

On tech policy, Toronto's Psiphon, built out of the University of Toronto's Citizen Lab to help people in Iran, Russia, and China evade censorship, told the Globe it has started drawing up plans to move its operations out of Canada, saying Bill C-22 would force it to compromise safety features protecting users in authoritarian countries. Bill C-22, the lawful access bill, would compel internet and telecom providers to build surveillance capability for police and CSIS, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. Ottawa says critics are misreading the bill. Companies including Signal and Apple have made similar noises in past months. Watch this if any of your clients hold positions in Canadian tech infrastructure, since a handful of firms relocating headquarters is now a live possibility, not just a threat.

Separately, the Globe reports Canadian diplomats say their children are still suffering lasting effects from Havana Syndrome, the mysterious illness first reported among foreign service families posted to Cuba back in 2017. It's a reminder Ottawa is still carrying unresolved liability and health costs from that file years later.

And CBC flags a growing backlog at Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada: a change in federal law last year let anyone with a Canadian ancestor apply for citizenship, and the resulting flood of applications is now trapping some Canadians born abroad who can't get home because their paperwork is stuck. If you have clients with family overseas trying to repatriate assets or relocate, this delay is worth flagging before they make moving plans.

None of the five items on today's broader watch list, the Bank of Canada rate decision, Dimensional Fund Advisors, Scotia Wealth Management, Manitoba Hydro, United Way Winnipeg, the Jets, or the Blue Bombers, came up in the federal political coverage today. Nothing to report there.

blocks.script:
On the other side of the AI security ledger, Google just paused its own open source bug bounty program entirely. Google engineers and open source maintainers were overwhelmed by reports that were invalid or contained hallucinations, and the company said the bug bounty program was paused as of October 1, with a promise to provide an update in the first quarter of 2027. The read for you: security teams across the industry are fighting the same flood of plausible sounding AI slop, and it is starting to clog the very systems meant to keep software safe.

Closer to home, BetaKit published a Canadian angle on the people behind AI. An anthropologist named Joseph Wilson spent time with so called ghost workers, the low paid human labellers who train these models, and with a Toronto chip company, to document the human labour hidden behind automated systems. It is a useful line for client conversations: every AI efficiency story has a labour story underneath it, and increasingly some of that labour is Canadian.

blocks.script:
The biggest health story today is about screens, not supplements. The Lancet published a three paper series on Sunday under the heading digital determinants of health, and it is the largest pooled analysis yet on this topic. A new umbrella review covering nine million people under 25 across 121 reviews finds consistent associations between problematic digital media use and a range of adverse health outcomes for children, adolescents and young adults. The key finding is not screen time as a raw number, it is what the researchers call problematic use, patterns that look like addiction rather than hours logged. Across all ages, obesity, nearsightedness, lower back pain, and cardiometabolic risk were linked to overall screen time across different age groups. In kids specifically, higher overall screen time was associated with poorer socio-emotional and cognitive development, increased anxiety and depression, and poorer sleep quality. One estimate in the series: spending more than two hours a day on screens could be associated with around 2.8 million healthy years of life lost to depression and 240,000 to obesity worldwide each year. The lead author was careful to say that estimate is intended to be illustrative of the possible scale of harm, so treat it as directional, not a precise count. CBC reports the researchers still want direct user data from the tech companies themselves before they call this settled.

Closer to home, CBC reports the mental health of young men in Canada is dropping, and the federal government opened a nationwide consultation this year to figure out why. Self reported rates of depression and anxiety among young men are climbing, and researchers point to the online manosphere content many young men are consuming as part of the problem. This is a government consultation, not a peer reviewed trial, so hold the causal story loosely. The self reported trend itself lines up with what clinicians have been flagging for a few years.

On the clinical research side, CBC covered a new study in the Canadian Medical Association Journal, the CMAJ, calling it the most comprehensive study yet of maternal health in Canada. The research looked at more than 108,000 in-hospital deliveries to Black people, and more than 1.3 million in-hospital deliveries to white people across the country between 2012 and 2023. Researchers found Black Canadians face a much higher risk of severe complications across pregnancy, labour, delivery and the postpartum period, including pre-eclampsia. Advocates are using the findings to push for mandatory race based data collection, something most provinces still do not do consistently.

On training, Outside has a piece on gyrotonic and gyrokinesis, movement systems built decades ago to get injured dancers back on stage, now getting adopted by hikers and trail runners for recovery. The method moves the spine and joints through slow, spiraling, resistance based patterns instead of isolated strength sets, the goal being to rebuild range of motion and coordination together rather than one after the other. This is built on decades of practitioner experience with dancers, not large randomized trials, so treat it as a useful complement to your normal strength and mobility work, not a replacement for either.

And if you want a weekend that forces actual rest, Outside also rounded up six ghost towns across the United States where you can book an overnight stay, old miners cabins in Montana, desert outposts in Nevada and California. Not a health study, just a reminder that a change of scenery with no cell signal is its own kind of recovery protocol.
talkingPoints: Lancet data suggests compulsive screen use, not raw hours, drives most of the harm in kids.
A CMAJ study now has hard numbers on Black maternal health gaps in Canada over a full decade.
Ottawa is consulting on why young men's mental health is sliding, worth watching for policy follow through.
Gyrotonic is moving from dance studios into trail recovery routines, a solid complement to strength work.
For a genuine digital detox weekend, there are bookable ghost towns south of the border.

blocks.title: Jets Win, Hellebuyck Stalemate, Bombers Fall From Playoff Spot
blocks.script:
The Winnipeg Jets picked up their first win of the season last night, beating the Red Wings in Detroit. That's on your watch list. Kyle Connor scored twice on the power play, and per the Globe and Mail, Winnipeg left Detroit still searching for its first win through two games. Jets goalie Stuart Skinner got the start after stopping 26 of 29 shots in Friday's opener, a 4-3 overtime loss to Boston where Connor also scored and piled up 14 shot attempts. Coach Scott Arniel says Connor is an elite player who, in his words, gets overlooked around the league. Two Winnipeg names are on the other bench too: former Jet Andrew Copp is centering Detroit's top line, and Manitoba's own Keegan Kolesar is suiting up for the Red Wings after being dealt from Vegas this summer. Winnipeg now moves on to Pittsburgh for Monday's game, the second stop on this road trip.

The bigger story trailing the Jets all month is Connor Hellebuyck. In a rare feat, he was named both the league's most valuable player and top goalie after the 2024-25 NHL season, when the Jets finished with the league's best record for the first time in franchise history. Now, the Jets formally suspended Hellebuyck for failure to report to training camp. GM Kevin Cheveldayoff says no doors are closed, that Hellebuyck is under contract for five years, but at the end of the day it's his choice. The asking price is believed to be a first-round pick, a top-six forward, and a goalie or prospect, and so far nobody's met it. The Globe and Mail argues the Jets and the Red Wings, who stripped captain Dylan Larkin of his letter after his own trade demand, need to make an example out of both situations, because the longer this drags on, the easier it gets for the next star to try the same move.

Now the Blue Bombers, also on your watch list, and the news is rough. Montreal clinched the East Division title with a 37-10 win over Winnipeg in front of a sellout crowd of 23,035 at Percival Molson Stadium. The Alouettes put up 564 yards of offense and buried Winnipeg early. Backup quarterback Dru Brown started in place of an injured Zach Collaros and is now winless in three career meetings against Montreal. Winnipeg can no longer win the West Division, and sits one game behind the last playoff spot with an elimination number of three. They host Calgary on October 10th, and that one matters.

Around the rest of the NHL: Seattle hammered Calgary 6-1 in the Kraken's home opener, Mackie Samoskevich scored twice and Joey Daccord made 32 saves, and the Flames are still winless. In New York, Igor Shesterkin made 28 saves and picked up an assist as the Rangers beat the Utah Mammoth, extending a point streak that includes a goal he scored earlier this year against Tampa. In Pittsburgh, Novak scored twice, including the overtime winner, as the Penguins beat the Canadiens 6-5. And in Ottawa, the Senators opened the post-Tkachuk era with a 3-2 win over Toronto, new captain Thomas Chabot picking up a goal and an assist in his first game wearing the C.

In the NFL, the Rams saved their best for last in a comeback win over Philadelphia. In Buffalo, Patriots quarterback Drake Maye threw three touchdown passes despite two turnovers to hand the Bills their first loss of the season, at their brand new stadium. Watch Kansas City too: The Athletic reports several team sources say the Chiefs are interested in signing free agent receiver Tyreek Hill, who hasn't played since a knee injury ended his season in Miami last year.

In the NBA, the Raptors fell 129-105 to Miami in the first-ever NBA game played in Quebec City. Toronto heads to Vancouver next weekend to play the Clippers in the second game of that series.

Tonight, the Jets are off before Monday night in Pittsburgh, and the NFL's Monday night game gives you one more data point on how this early season is shaking out.
